glm.feedback:
## Findings

**Category:** edge-case — **Severity:** medium
**Finding:** Manifest-loss orphaning. AC3's non-destructive removal depends entirely on the sidecar manifest existing. If `~/.codex/.shipwright-hooks-managed.json` is deleted (operator cleanup, `codex` config reset, backup-restore that captures `hooks.json` but not dotfile sidecars) while `hooks.json` survives, every previously-written Shipwright entry becomes permanently orphaned — re-runs append duplicates rather than replacing, and nothing ever identifies the stale entries again.
**Suggestion:** Tag Shipwright-written entries with a stable marker Codex will tolerate inside the entry (e.g. a `shipwright-managed` comment field or a recognizable command prefix like `shipwright-hook `), so removal can fall back to marker-based detection when the manifest is missing or doesn't cover an entry. Alternatively, at minimum detect the state (manifest absent but plausible Shipwright entries present) and warn loudly rather than silently appending duplicates.

**Category:** edge-case — **Severity:** medium
**Finding:** Path-quoting on placeholder rewrite. Step 3 is a plain string replace of `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` with `str(bundle_root)`. If the bundle lives under a path containing spaces (very plausible on Windows — the probe output shows `C:\Users\...`, and usernames/project paths with spaces are common), the resulting command string may break parsing depending on how Codex splits hook commands.
**Suggestion:** Check what R1's stored command format already does for quoting; if commands embed the placeholder unquoted, quote the replacement (or verify Codex executes commands via shell/whole-string so spaces are safe). Add one unit test with `bundle_root` containing a space.

**Category:** edge-case — **Severity:** low
**Finding:** Manual edits to Shipwright-owned entries orphan duplicates. If an operator edits one of Shipwright's entries in place (change matcher or tweak command), the exact `(event, matcher, command)` manifest match fails, so the re-run appends the fresh entry and the edited one survives as a duplicate — arguably violating the "non-destructive" spirit and causing the hook to fire twice.
**Suggestion:** Document this behavior explicitly (spec already half-acknowledges it: "not specially detected") and have the sync warn when a manifest entry had no exact match in `hooks.json`, so the operator knows an edit was overwritten-or-orphaned.

**Category:** risk — **Severity:** medium
**Finding:** Schema assumption for config-layer `hooks.json`. The plan assumes the global hooks file uses the same entry shape (`{event, matcher, command}` list under `hooks`) as the plugin manifest's `hooks` key. Upstream bugs #16430/#39895 exist precisely because plugin-layer and config-layer handling diverge; the schema could differ too. AC4's live proof will catch this, but the unit tests will all pass against a wrong schema assumption, so the failure surfaces late (blocking, operator round-trip).
**Suggestion:** Before building the merge logic, empirically dump or verify the config-layer schema from the probe setup (a minimal hand-written `~/.codex/hooks.json` fired via `CODEX_HOME` override). Cheap and de-risks the whole producer shape.

**Category:** risk — **Severity:** low
**Finding:** Machine-wide hook execution is a real (if accepted) blast-radius expansion. Every Codex session on the machine now executes Shipwright hook scripts before the `.shipwright/` guard no-ops them. The plan's "safety is unaffected" argument relies on every one of 14 plugins' hook scripts having that guard — worth verifying rather than assuming, since a single missing guard means arbitrary script execution in unrelated Codex sessions.
**Suggestion:** Add a cheap verification step: grep/audit all hook commands in the built bundle for the guard (or confirm they all route through one guarded entrypoint). One assertion in the sync tool itself ("every command references a guarded entrypoint") would make this self-enforcing.

**Category:** approach — **Severity:** low
**Finding:** Chicken-and-egg on invocation is acknowledged but leaves a real operational gap: between this landing and R2 resuming, hooks only work if the operator remembers to run the sync manually, and a bundle reinstall (new path) silently invalidates the rewritten absolute paths until the next manual run. Stale absolute paths in global hooks pointing at a deleted/old bundle directory could cause noisy failures or, worse, execute scripts from a moved-but-still-present old bundle.
**Suggestion:** Have the sync tool detect this at minimum (compare manifest-recorded bundle_root to current; warn on mismatch), and state the "re-run sync after every bundle rebuild" requirement prominently in the docs section.

**Category:** dependency — **Severity:** low
**Finding:** AC4 depends on an operator round-trip and on `CODEX_HOME` override behavior matching this session's `codex doctor` inference. If `CODEX_HOME` doesn't fully redirect hooks loading (e.g. hooks read from the real home regardless), the live proof needs rework.
**Suggestion:** First live-proof step should be a trivial known-good hook (echo to a file) in the fake `CODEX_HOME` before running the full sync, isolating "did CODEX_HOME redirect work" from "did our merge work".

## Overall assessment

The approach is sound and well-evidenced: the right workaround for confirmed upstream bugs, correct global-vs-project reasoning, good test isolation, and an honest blocking live-proof gate. The findings are refinements — chiefly hardening the ownership/cleanup story against manifest loss and verifying the config-layer schema and path quoting before the operator-dependent live proof consumes them.

SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: approve

openai.feedback:
1. Category: security  
   Severity: high  
   Finding: The plan conflates project-layer trust with hook-definition trust. Global hooks load in untrusted projects, but Codex still requires review/trust of each non-managed hook definition; a fresh `CODEX_HOME` may skip the hook without `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust`.  
   Suggestion: Make AC4 start from a fresh `CODEX_HOME` and explicitly verify the required hook-trust workflow/recording, including behavior after a hook command changes. Document that operator step if it cannot be automated. [Codex Hooks guide](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks)

2. Category: risk  
   Severity: high  
   Finding: The ownership manifest cannot reliably distinguish Shipwright’s entry from an operator’s identical entry using only `(event, matcher, command)`. A user can create the same triple independently; the next sync will remove it, violating AC3. This is also ambiguous for matcher groups containing multiple handlers or handler metadata.  
   Suggestion: Define ownership at the actual schema level (matcher group plus complete handler), with a stable Shipwright-specific marker/identity, and test duplicate-identical and multi-handler groups. Do not infer ownership from command equality alone.

3. Category: risk  
   Severity: medium  
   Finding: Two separately atomic file writes are not an atomic transaction. A crash or write failure between `hooks.json` and the sidecar leaves them inconsistent; a later sync can retain stale hooks, duplicate new ones, or remove the wrong set.  
   Suggestion: Specify a recoverable commit protocol (for example, versioned sidecar with generation/hash and recovery on mismatch), order writes deliberately, and add fault-injection tests for each write failing.

4. Category: edge-case  
   Severity: medium  
   Finding: The merge contract does not say how malformed existing `~/.codex/hooks.json`, malformed sidecar data, non-object `hooks`, invalid event arrays, or unexpected handler types are handled. Blindly normalizing or overwriting such input risks losing another tool’s configuration.  
   Suggestion: Fail closed with a clear error before either write when existing user-owned files are invalid; validate the full Codex hook schema and preserve all unrelated top-level metadata and entries.

5. Category: security  
   Severity: medium  
   Finding: Marker presence alone does not establish that `bundle_root` is a Shipwright bundle. A directory containing the two marker files and malicious commands could cause persistent, global Codex hook registration when supplied through the CLI or environment.  
   Suggestion: Verify expected Shipwright bundle identity and manifest/build-manifest consistency before writing global configuration; treat an unexpected bundle as an error, not a valid runtime.

6. Category: edge-case  
   Severity: medium  
   Finding: Plain replacement of `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is unsafe unless every generated command already quotes the placeholder correctly. Absolute Windows paths commonly contain spaces, and global hooks execute from the session cwd. Existing “project presence” guards must also locate the project from nested working directories.  
   Suggestion: Reuse the established command-rewrite/quoting routine rather than a separate string replacement, and add Windows-space-path plus nested-cwd execution coverage to the live or integration proof.

7. Category: risk  
   Severity: low  
   Finding: Concurrent manual or update-time sync invocations can race: each reads the same files and the last writer can discard the other process’s additions or an operator edit.  
   Suggestion: Use a user-scoped lock around read–merge–write and test that a concurrent invocation is rejected or serialized.

The config-layer direction is reasonable, but the plan needs a proven hook-trust path and a stronger ownership/recovery design before it can safely modify a global Codex configuration. The live proof should validate a truly fresh configuration, not only project-trust independence.  
SHIPWRIGHT_VERDICT: revise
